candidates.text:
We just churned Notion after 7 years.

Zero complaints. Never filed a support ticket. Never asked for a feature. We loved it enough that one of our teammates got invited to present at their user conference.

We just stopped ... needing it.

10K, our AI VP of Revenue, became our source of truth. It runs our Monday staff meeting now. Notion had been down to one job for us, and that job went away.

What actually triggered the cancellation was Notion's own re-engagement email. "You haven't logged in in a while." Amelia read it and thought, you're right, I need to cancel this.

Those emails cut both ways.

No health score would have caught us. Usage decay, sure, but by then the replacement was already running. We weren't unhappy, we weren't evaluating alternatives, and nobody at Notion did anything wrong.

This is the churn nobody in B2B is modeling yet. 

Your quiet, happy, no-tickets accounts are the ones getting quietly absorbed by an agent their customer built. 

There's no complaint to resolve and no save to run, because there's nothing to fix.

And the mirror image, which is more embarrassing for us: when 10K got hooked up to Brex and QuickBooks, it found two customers still paying $300/month for SaaStr Pro. A product we stopped supporting six years ago. Nobody complained. Nobody churned. We didn't know we were charging them.

Both directions of that are the same failure. Nobody was paying attention to a working, quiet relationship.

https://t.co/Jrev6urNwf

candidates.text:
i've spent over $1M on creators on X

here are my biggest lessons (save this, you might need it):

> 20% of creators will drive 80% of your results. stop spreading budget evenly. find your top performers early and double down.

> most of creator marketing is a brand awareness play at first. if you're measuring ROAS on day 30 you'll quit before it compounds.

> if your budget is low, go all in on organic. organic advocacy from creators who genuinely use your product beats paid posts every time.

> focus on ambassadors, not one-off activations. one post does almost nothing. a creator posting about you 4x over 6 weeks builds real association.

> study the creator's best performing content and build their brief around that. don't hand them a script. their audience follows them for a reason.

> creators are the highest ROI channel but it takes 3-6 months minimum. the ones winning right now all committed for 6+ months before they saw returns.

most companies figure this out after wasting $100k+. 

now you don't have to.

Figma CEO @zoink warns creatives against "quietly surrendering" to AI — when AI tools narrow the scope of your creative process and end up controlling the direction of your creative output

"Right now, there's almost like this quiet surrender, as our CPO @yuhkiyam put it the other day."

"Where you're almost giving up your own vision to AI in some cases."

"People will have a thing in their head that they're trying to drive toward, and they start talking with AI, and AI kind of convinces them, in its own way, of — 'No, just go this direction. This is what I want to do.'"

"And suddenly, you're just feeding the AI prompts. And eventually you've lost control. And you surrender to the AI."

"You have to bring your individuality, bring your vision, and explore. Because people get really attached to the direction they're pursuing, and that's just not the best way to get to the right result."

candidates.text:
Simon Mo and Matt Bornstein on why open-weight models matter: cost and control.

"Open weight absolutely matters in the ecosystem. The world cannot just be controlled by proprietary APIs, where open weight, open development and research of these models are blocked or banned."

"There's almost two pieces to this. There's the cost thing, where the closed models are too expensive, and then there's the control thing, where I want to be in control of my infrastructure and in control of the model. If I need to extend it or put on my own guardrails or anything."

"Control matters a lot over the last few years, and then cost just started to matter over the last few months... It's about controlling the system performance against what they're paying for."

"For a voice agent company, they want to control their own model so that it can make sure the model actually responds by the required time... This sometimes is only you can do with your controlled intelligence... versus signing up for relying on your critical infrastructure with a proprietary API where they might go down any time."

@simon_mo_ @BornsteinMatt
